title: Trump Says He's in 'Deciding Mode' on Iran as Tehran Sends Terms via Qatar
excerpt: The president outlined three paths — "wiping Iran out, letting them rot economically or making a deal" — while saying he would "probably" meet Iran's president at the UN General Assembly.
body:
• US President Donald Trump told Fox News on Sunday he is in "deciding mode" on Iran and that "very big things" will happen in the near future, laying out three options: "wiping Iran out, letting them rot economically or making a deal."
  • Trump's remarks — including "if and when do I blow the entire nation up? They better behave" — come three days after he told Axios he was weighing whether to "annihilate" Iran, as the US-Iran war approaches 204 days with no US strikes publicly reported for over two weeks.
  • Tehran has sent a seven-point list of conditions via Qatari mediators — including an end to the naval blockade and the release of frozen funds — while Iran's military warned US regional allies they would be considered "complicit" if American strikes resume.
  • Trump said he would "probably" meet Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian at the UN General Assembly this week, even as the State Department warned Americans across the region that the conflict "has the potential to escalate rapidly."

US President Donald Trump signalled on Sunday that Washington is weighing its next move in the war with Iran, telling Fox News chief foreign correspondent Trey Yingst that he is in "deciding mode" and that "very big things" will happen in the near future — as Tehran laid out its terms for talks through Qatari intermediaries.

What Trump said

According to Yingst, reporting on Fox & Friends Weekend, Trump described three strategies under consideration: "wiping Iran out, letting them rot economically or making a deal." Then came the line Tehran was meant to hear: "My question is, if and when do I blow the entire nation up? They better behave."

The remarks build on what Trump told Axios on Thursday — that he is considering whether to "go in and annihilate them," referring to the Iranian regime, adding that anything "could happen with me."

"My question is, if and when do I blow the entire nation up? They better behave."

— President Donald Trump, in remarks to Fox News

Iran's conditions and warnings

On Saturday, Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, told Al Jazeera that Tehran had conveyed its conditions for ending the war to Qatari mediators and was "awaiting President Trump's response." The reported seven-point list includes an end to the war on all fronts, the release of Iran's frozen funds, an end to the US naval blockade, sanctions relief, a prisoner release, and restrictions on foreign interference in Iran's nuclear program.

"It is in Washington's interest to accept these conditions. Trump's threats will not achieve any results. We are prepared for a decisive war," Rezaei said. Iran's central military command said Sunday it had received information suggesting the US could be preparing new military action, and warned — via the semi-official Tasnim news agency — that any new US attack would trigger sustained strikes on US bases and interests across the region, with assisting countries considered parties to the conflict. There have been no publicly reported US strikes on Iran for more than two weeks.

The diplomatic backdrop

Trump has not closed the door on negotiation. He is expected to meet six Persian Gulf leaders on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly this week, and his administration will allow a "core delegation" of Iranian officials — including President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi — to attend. Asked whether he would meet Pezeshkian, Trump answered "probably," according to Yingst.

But the security picture is darkening. On Saturday, the State Department warned the conflict "has the potential to escalate rapidly" and advised heightened vigilance for Americans across the region. The US Embassy in Saudi Arabia restricted government personnel travel to Taif and Yanbu after Iran-backed Houthis claimed missile and drone attacks on sites in Riyadh and an Aramco oil facility in Yanbu. Trump cut short a Camp David visit on Sunday without explanation.

Why this matters for the diaspora

For the Indian diaspora, the stakes are direct. Millions of Indians live and work in the Gulf states now in the shadow of escalation; a widening war would put Indian workers, businesses, and families across the region at immediate risk. Surging energy prices also hit India — the world's third-largest oil importer — hard, squeezing household budgets and remittance-dependent families alike.

What's next

All eyes are on the UN General Assembly: whether Trump meets Pezeshkian, how Gulf leaders respond to his three options, and whether the Qatari-mediated channel produces anything beyond conditions and counter-conditions. With the war at 204 days and Tehran warning of "painful attacks" if strikes resume, the "deciding mode" Trump describes could resolve as negotiation — or as the escalation he keeps threatening.
